chunks: And beware of depending upon hopes,
for they are the mainstay of fools. Intellect is the preservation of experiences, and the best of what you have experienced is that which teaches you a lesson.
Seize the opportunity before it becomes a cause of grief.
Not every seeker achieves (what he seeks), and not every departed one returns.
And among the corruptions is wasting one's provision, and ruining one's destination (the Hereafter).
And every matter has a consequence. What is destined for you will shortly come to you.
A trader undertakes a risk. Often a small quantity is more beneficial than a large quantity!
There is no good in an ignoble helper, nor in a suspicious friend.
Be compliant with the world as long as its riding beast is subdued for you,
and do not put yourself to risk in expectation of more than that.
And beware lest the feeling of enmity (or stubbornness) should gallop you away.
ai.seo_question: What are the key ethical teachings regarding experience and opportunity in Nahj al-Balagha?
ai.summary: Delivered by Imam Ali to his son Hasan following the Battle of Siffin, this passage employs merchant metaphors to illustrate the volatility of worldly affairs and the necessity of intellectual prudence. It underscores the Shia emphasis on *'aql* (intellect) as the guardian of experience, warning that passive reliance on hope (*al-manā*) leads to ruin, while active vigilance ensures one capitalizes on fleeting opportunities before they become sources of regret.
